_comment: Composite indexes, in the order the planner needs them: equality-filtered fields first,
then the field the query sorts on. Field order is not interchangeable — an index built
the other way round will not serve the query it was built for.
Auto-indexing is left ON, so a query we did not anticipate still runs (and says so in
auto_indexed) rather than failing. These are declared anyway because the first call of
each one is the one a person is waiting on, and because writing them down is the only
record of what this app actually asks the datastore for.
Every console query carries an extra `owner_uid = $auth.uid` filter that the row rules
AND in server-side — which is why the console indexes lead with owner_uid and the
function's own (organization-level, no rules) do not.
The `member:` entries serve the second branch of a shared board's read rule — `project_id in
$auth.claims.boards` — which the platform plans as a separate query with its own index. Declare
them: auto-indexing on hosted altengine builds only ONE missing index per call, so a read whose
two branches both lack one fails the first time it is asked (fixed in the platform at
altengineapp 9ac661a, not yet deployed at the time of writing).

duties.for: the scheduler: the runnable queue, highest priority then oldest first

THE OTHER HALF OF THE MUTEX. `holder` is '<project>:<agent>' while a duty is active and null otherwise, so one agent cannot hold two duties: the second claim's transaction is refused outright. The board is in the value because agent ids are only unique within a board. Nulls do not collide, so any number of duties may be unheld.
console: one board column, most recently touched first
console: the Queued column, in the order the scheduler will take them — the same order as the index above it, so the top of that column is the duty an agent claims next
member: a board column or the working set, read by someone the board is shared with

THE PARALLEL LIMIT. `lane` is '<project>#<n>' while a duty is active on a board with runner.parallel set, and null otherwise, so two claims racing for the last free lane cannot both land. The function creates this on demand too.
the function: is a rules duty already open on this board
the function: is a setup duty already open for this machine
the function: the duties waiting behind one that finished, deleted or failed
the function: whether a board has a setup unfinished, which holds every other claim

THE MUTEX FOR RECURRING DUTIES. A duty filed by a schedule carries '<schedule>@<due>'; every other duty carries nothing, and nulls do not collide. Two ticks racing over one occurrence — the function's own cron and a polling machine — write two different duty rows with the same value, so the second transaction is refused whole and the occurrence files exactly one duty.
the function: what one schedule has filed, newest first

threads.for: the function: a duty's decision log
console: the same log, read directly
member: the same log, read by someone the board is shared with

tokens.for: the function: a board's agent tokens

attachments.for: the function: the files on one duty, oldest first
the function: sweeping a board's files when it is deleted

agents.for: console: which agents are working this board
member: the same strip; also the function's own board/open

THE MUTEX, not a query. Two agents cannot both hold one duty because the datastore refuses the second write of the same active_duty_id, which fails that whole claim transaction and leaves the duty untouched. Nulls do not collide, so any number of agents may be idle. The function creates this on demand too (see store.ensureUniqueIndex) — auto-indexing would never make it, because what a query needs is never unique.

machines.for: the function: a machine by the id the console knows it by
THE PAIRING MUTEX: one pairing becomes at most one machine, however many polls race for its key

pairings.for: the function: the pairing a person typed the code of; unique so a code names one machine
the function: sweeping pairings nobody finished

machine_links.for: the function: the boards one machine works
the function: the machines on one board
the function: one person's machines on a board, when they leave it

machine_requests.for: the function: what one machine has been asked to set up
the function: sweeping a deleted board's requests

memberships.for: the function: the boards one person is a member of — their claim, and their board list
the function: a board's members, oldest first; also the sweep when a board is deleted

push_subscriptions.for: the function: the devices one person gets notifications on

schedules.for: the tick: every board's recurring duties that are due, soonest first. The one query a cron run makes when there is nothing to do, so it must be served by an index rather than scanned.
the same, for one board — what a polling machine runs for the boards it works, when the function's own cron was never set
the function: a board's schedules, for the console and for deleting a board
the function: which schedule filed a duty that just finished, so the next run can be told how it went
